title: Pull-away: on it, with it, pull away, shoot
summary: How pull-away works in four beats, which targets it often suits, and the two typical faults: riding the target and stopping the push.

body.html: In pull-away the muzzles first join the target, then pull ahead of it. It is widely taught by British coaches. Coaches do not all give the lead methods the same names. A name taken from a coaching school can mean pull-away for one coach and swing-through for another, so ask your coach which is meant. Step by step, it looks like this:
The muzzles start on the target, then pull ahead; the lead you see is smaller than the actual lead.
body.heading: Watch how the lead works

html: “On it”: the gun is mounted onto the target or its front edge; the muzzles touch it on its line.
“With it”: the muzzles track the target for a moment at its speed, matching line and pace.
“Pull away”: the gun accelerates smoothly ahead until the right lead picture appears.
“Shoot”: the trigger is pulled while the gun is still accelerating or moving.
Follow-through: the gun keeps going after the shot.

body.html: Strengths: you follow the target for a moment before pulling ahead. That gives you a feel for its speed, distance and path before you decide to fire, so the barrels stay well on its line. It suits long targets, quartering targets (flying at an angle away from or towards you) and rising targets. Because of the acceleration, the lead you see is smaller than with maintained lead.
Weaknesses: the amount of acceleration varies from target to target, so it takes practice to feel it. Tracking for too long becomes “riding the target”, and stopping the push gives a miss behind.
Coaches say “touch it and go”, “mount on it and push out”, or the four-beat “on it, with it, pull away, shoot”.

notes.html: Keep the four-beat rhythm when you translate: it matters more than the exact words.

phrases.speaker: coach
phrases.en: On it, with it, pull away, shoot.
phrases.meaning: Join the target, track it, accelerate ahead, fire.

phrases.speaker: coach
phrases.meaning: Meet the target with the muzzles and immediately start pulling ahead.

phrases.speaker: coach
phrases.meaning: The shooter tracked the target for too long before pulling away and lost the line or the moment.

phrases.speaker: coach
phrases.en: Mount on it and push out a bit more.
phrases.meaning: Mount onto the target, then pull a little further ahead before firing.

key_points.html: Muzzles start on the target (or its front edge).
Track at its speed, then accelerate ahead.
Trigger while the gun is still moving forward; then follow through.
Good line control; suits long, quartering and rising targets.

quiz.q: In pull-away, what happens just before the trigger is pulled?

options.text: The gun stops on the target
The gun accelerates ahead of the target
The gun drops below the target
The gun waits at the break point

quiz.explain: The pull-away itself is the acceleration ahead; the shot is fired while the gun is still moving forward.

quiz.q: The coach says “You rode it too long”. What went wrong?

options.text: He stood too long on the stand before calling
He mounted the gun far too early
He tracked it too long before pulling away
The trapper released the target late

quiz.explain: “Riding the target” means following it too long, so it slows, drops or escapes and the line is lost.

quiz.q: Compared with maintained lead, the perceived lead in pull-away is usually…

options.text: smaller, because the acceleration adds lead
larger, because the gun starts on the target
zero, with no gap at all

quiz.explain: The brief acceleration carries the gun forward during the shot delay, so less gap needs to be seen.
